analysis.title: US Market Intelligence | Morning Briefing (October 19, 2026)
key_insights: JPM stays tactically bullish after last week's sell-off (SPX -2.0%, NDX -5.5%). It says the AI-led sell-off was driven by Momentum/Tech Unwind and AI Credit Fears, while earnings (ASML, TSMC) and consumer data stayed healthy and no earnings deterioration has shown up so far.

Last week's move looked like rotation more than broad liquidation: 7 of 11 SPX sectors rose, led by Staples and Energy (+5.0% each) and Health Care (+3.4%). The sell-off began after China's ChangXin Memory said it would launch a denser server memory chip.

JPM does not expect the rotation out of Tech to end abruptly, though the pace could moderate. It favors cyclical exposure outside Tech and selectively buying Tech weakness, especially Semis and Memory, through defined-risk options structures.
Large-cap Banks are an area of interest. Earnings were generally positive, and the recent pullback could offer a way to participate in a recovery in XLF (XLF was up about 1.4% on the week).

Rates: Treasuries rallied and the curve bull-flattened despite hawkish CPI and PPI. The 2/5/10/30-year yields fell 11/17/19/20bp, and the 10Y posted its biggest weekly decline since August 2025. JPM reads this as flight to quality as AI equity valuation concerns spilled into bonds.

Key catalysts: the inflation component of this week's PMIs, the Oct 28 Fed meeting (a hold would remove residual near-term hike risk, but the focus is on remarks about the FY27 policy path), rates vol moderation, and META earnings and NVDA GTC Berlin as tests of AI revenue delivery.

Monetization Menu (Oct 19): prefers a more selective approach. It keeps a preference for Tech and a rebound via pairs trades and derivatives, is constructive on Financials and Retailers, favors Brazil and Japan, and is monitoring Reopening opportunities that would benefit from lower energy prices and rotation away from AI.

AI credit: hyperscaler spreads widened 12bp last week to 148bp (widest since July 2026) and JULI sector-weighted dispersion rose to 21.2bp (highest since May 2025). Strategist Nathaniel Rosenbaum reads this as investors demanding more compensation for lower-rated, capital-intensive issuers. Ratings have not deteriorated, and he sees the widening as overdone unless earnings show fundamental weakness.

The credit trading desk (Christian Crosby) says funding stress now sits with levered borrowers (neoclouds, data center project finance, GPU deals). Higher borrowing costs and weaker equities compound each other, and a growing list of pulled or delayed IPOs raises concern that converts and secondary rounds could dry up.

Rates view (Jay Barry): last week's UST move had three possible drivers, AI equity valuation concerns, cleaner positioning (Treasury Client Survey longs at the lowest since August), and Treasury possibly leaving the door open to long-end issuance cuts. He recommends tactical 10s/30s steepeners.

Broadening: JPM favors SPW over RTY, citing stronger aggregate earnings power and less refinancing exposure. Elevated yields remain a headwind for RTY even if an unwind of +QQQ/-IWM positions helps it.

Hedging: the Dispersion Index rose from about 30 at its September low to about 37, still below its July peak. If dispersion keeps rising, passive sector ETFs may become less effective hedges for single-stock exposure, which could favor D1 baskets.

Positioning: HF performance drawdown deepened to -2.1% MTD globally (Eq L/S -2.3%, Quants -1% to -2%, Multi-Strats -2%), with APAC the weakest at -3.8% MTD. Multi-Strat de-grossing was close to the worst in two years, while US positioning stayed around the 40th percentile.

Crowding remains in places: AI Core Revenue positioning is at the 94th percentile (12m) and 99th (LT), Semis L/S is about 3.0x versus Software about 1x, and Utilities are heavily under-owned (HF positioning near 10-year lows).

JPM sees the current setup as echoing 2023 more than 2018. 3Q26 US 10yr is +82bps versus +73bps in 3Q23, and oil is up more than 40% versus about 30%. HFs are about +6% YTD and equities about +13% MXWD / +14% SPX, so JPM thinks stabilization and a 4Q rally are more likely than not.

Morning snapshot: SPX +0.5%, NDX +1.0%, RTY +0.4%, WTI $101.11, 10Y 5.081%, VIX 18.67. Overnight AI headlines were mixed: Nscale IPO valuation pressure after MSFT exited a UK data center deal, and Anthropic offering BX a yield above 10% to anchor a $60B TPU-backed debt package.
Europe is lower, with France lagging amid Russia/Ukraine escalation and protests. China Q3 GDP printed +4.5% YoY versus 4.4% survey, with Retail Sales +1.1% versus 0.5% survey.

This week brings a busy reporting slate, with META (Oct 21) and NVDA's GTC Berlin (Oct 20-22) the key tests of AI revenue delivery, spending plans and demand visibility.

Earnings this week: Oct 19 AGNC, CLF, FITB, STLD. Oct 20 includes GE, GM, COF, NFLX, RTX, UAL, ISRG. Oct 21 includes META, TSLA, IBM, TXN, LRCX, T, NEE. Oct 22 includes BX, HON, LMT, PG, UNP, NEM, WDC. Oct 23 includes AXP, SLB.

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings from ASML and TSMC were healthy, consumer data is resilient, and no earnings deterioration has appeared. JPM expects a stabilization and 4Q rally, as in 2023.
tension_points.bear_case: AI credit fears, a Momentum/Tech Unwind and crowded positioning (AI Core Revenue at the 94th-99th percentile) could extend the sell-off, and the 2018 analog is a risk.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Upcoming earnings that reveal fundamental weakness (META results, NVDA GTC Berlin) or a renewed spike in yields and rates vol.

tension_points.bull_case: Rosenbaum sees the widening as overdone, since ratings have not deteriorated and issuance was concentrated among higher-rated borrowers.
tension_points.bear_case: The credit desk says funding costs for levered neoclouds, data center project finance and GPU deals are reflexive, and pulled or delayed IPOs could dry up funding.
